chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Ali ibn Mahziyar who said:

'Abdullah ibn Muhammad wrote to Abu Al-Hasan (peace be upon him), 'May I be sacrificed for you! Some of your mawali allege that when a man speaks with Zahaar, the expiation becomes obligatory upon him, whether he violates the oath or not, and they say that his violation is his speaking with Zahaar, and the expiation is made upon him as a punishment for the speech; and some of them allege that the expiation does not become obligatory upon him until he violates the matter upon which he swore, so if he violates it, the expiation becomes obligatory upon him, and otherwise there is no expiation upon him.'
So he (peace be upon him) signed with his own handwriting: 'The expiation is not obligatory until the violation becomes obligatory.'

key_terms.الظِّهَار: Zahaar: A form of divorce where a husband likens his wife's back to his mother's back.
key_terms.الكَفَّارَة: Kaffarah: Expiation or atonement required for specific acts.
key_terms.الْحِنْث: Hinth: Violation or breaking of an oath/pledge.

ai.seo_question: When does the expiation for Zahaar become obligatory in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This correspondence from Abdullah ibn Muhammad to Imam al-Rida (AS) resolves a juristic dispute regarding whether the expiation for Zahaar is triggered by the mere utterance of the formula or by the subsequent violation of the oath (hinth). The Imam’s concise verdict, 'Expiation is not obligatory until the violation becomes obligatory,' establishes that the legal penalty is contingent upon the actual breach of the condition, distinguishing the linguistic act from its binding legal consequence. This ruling underscores the Shia principle that penalties in Islamic law require specific conditions of actualization rather than mere potentiality.

en.hubeali: Muhammad Bin Yahya, from Ahmad Bin Muhammad, from Ali Bin Mahziyar who said,

‘Abu Abdullah Bin Muhammad wrote to Abu Al-Hassanasws, ‘May I be sacrificed for youasws! Some of the ones in yourasws Wilayah are alleging that the man, when he speaks with the Zahaar, the expiation is Obligated upon him, violating an oath or not violating an oath, and they are saying that his lie is his speaking with the Zahaar, and rather the expiation is made to be upon him as a Punishment for the speech; and one of them is alleging that the expiation does not necessitate until he is lying regarding something which he has sworn upon, for the lying Obligates the expiation upon him, or else there is no expiation upon him’.
So he<sup>asws</sup> signed by his<sup>asws</sup> own handwriting: ‘The expiation is not Obligated until the violation of a vow occurs’.
en.sarwar: 19. Muhammad ibn Yahya has narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Ali ibn Mahziyar from who has said the following: “

‘Abd Allah ibn Muhammad once wrote to abu al-Hassan, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, saying, ‘I pray to Allah to keep my soul in service for your cause, certain ones of your followers think that if a man speaks the statement of al-Zihar, then expiation becomes due, violating the swearing or not. They say that its sinfulness and violation is in the very statement of al-Zihar and expiation is as penalty for such statement. Certain others think that expiation is not due unless swearing is violated in something about which he swears, and if he violates then expiation is due on him, otherwise, there is no expiation.
He (the Imam), ‘Alayhi al-Salam, signed the answer in his own handwriting that said, ‘Expiation does not become obligatory until violation of oath occurs.”’
